subjects.displayTitle: Desire and discernment: recovering the freedom to choose
subjects.introduction: A king may conquer East and West, his name a terror to other rulers, and still be a horse ridden by his own greed and lust. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s picture of a conqueror who cannot govern himself opens a question that outward success never settles: what actually commands a life? Desire here is more than bodily appetite. It includes avarice, pride, self-serving speech, and the expectations that veil a person from recognising truth when it arrives in an unhoped-for form; Bahá’u’lláh observes that when one veil is torn away a larger one is often found behind it. The qualities that are no fault in an animal become sins in a human being, because a human being can choose, and the commanding self gives no respite unless divine protection is sought. Epictetus advised pausing before an anticipated pleasure to consider its aftermath [1], an exercise of attention that sits beside the Bahá’í reliance on knowledge, love, education and prayer. The severity of the teaching is matched by its confidence that something precious lies hidden beneath the clay, like steel in ore. From here the inquiry turns to chastity and purity, and to the harm of unchastity.
subjects.arc: Begin with power unable to master itself, examine desire’s effects on judgment and conduct, then turn toward knowledge, education, and the disclosure of hidden capacities.

order.why: Consider the persistence of one veil after another.
Open with the ruler who is himself ruled.
shortened: Consider the condition of a King who has overcome and conquered the East and the West, whose fame has encircled the globe, whose very name strikes terror at the hearts of other rulers but his reason ruled by passion and his heart defeated by greed and list, He is like unto a horse on whose back these malevolent qualities are riding, causing him to gallop through marshy fields of heedlessness and craggy heights of egotism.

order.why: Ask whether understanding is grounded in reality.
Examine expectations as a veil before recognition.
shortened: It is the veil of idle imaginations which, in the days of the Manifestations of the Unity of God and the Daysprings of His everlasting glory, hath intervened, and will continue to intervene, between them and the rest of mankind. For in those days, He Who is the Eternal Truth manifesteth Himself in conformity with that which He Himself hath purposed, and not according to the desires and expectations of men.

order.why: Join the warning about appetite with the warning about names.
Read the varied ways desire can misdirect a life.
shortened: Among the people are those who have turned away from the truth by following the creation, and among them are those who have gone astray in the valley of passions after We showed them this exalted path, and among them are those who are occupied with wealth, heedless of their final end, and among them are those who gather but know not for whom they gather - verily they do not understand.

order.why: Consider the reported account of a life organized around gratification.
shortened: Abdul-Baha answered: "In the world of humanity, every person is stimulated by a certain objective point.

The objective point of a forth soul is to satisfy his selfish appetites and lust. He thinks of no other things save those elements which might contribute to the gratification of his animal propensities.

order.why: Distinguish animal instinct from human moral responsibility.
shortened: All sin is prompted by the dictates of nature.  These dictates of nature, which are among the hallmarks of corporeal existence, are not sins with respect to the animal but are sins with regard to man.  The animal is the source of imperfections such as anger, lust, envy, greed, cruelty, and pride.  All these blameworthy qualities are found in the nature of the animal, and do not constitute sins with regard to the animal, whereas they are sins with regard to man.

order.why: Read captivity to nature as the starting difficulty.
shortened: O seeker of truth! Human souls are absorbed in desires and passions and are captives of the world of nature.

order.why: Consider the need for divine assistance in the struggle.
shortened: O servant of the Most Glorious Beauty! What you wrote is truly the exact reality. Man is constantly under the dominion of the commanding self. It gives not a moment's opportunity nor grants any respite before the hosts of passion and desire launch their assault. What can poor man do alone and solitary against this endless army, unless the protection and shelter of the Divine Unity provides a solution and guards against the evil of this cruel oppressor?

order.why: Keep the reported sentence about temptation in its source form.
Read the explanation of momentary indulgence.
Consider the connection with moderation.
Ask what forms of inward wealth are being overlooked.
Read the warning about a life exhausted by worldly pursuit.
shortened: The dwellers of this ephemeral world, high and low alike, spend their days and nights in pursuit of worldly matters only to suffer, in the end, manifest loss.

order.why: Compare two uses of a limited lifetime.
shortened: Days in any case come to an end, but there is a great difference between them. One person's life passes in the defilement of lusts, while another's time passes in hardship and difficulty in the path of the Lord of Signs. How great is the difference between them!

order.why: Consider the consequences described as regret and despair.
shortened: But if he indulgeth in his passions and desires, he will be hopeless, fall into deep despair, experience profound regret, and become afflicted with the torment of hell.

order.why: Read the image of a life dissipated.
shortened: Those who dissipate their lives by lust and passion cause their souls to drown in the whirlpools of this world.

order.why: Retain the warning about descending into passion.
Keep the further image of immersion in darkness.
shortened: They have conceived a transient fireplace to be an eternal garden and known an extinguished candle as a radiant flame.

Therefore they have become immersed in passions and drowned in the sea of darkness. They have become content with a putrid drop of fleeting life and turned away from eternal life in the Most Glorious Kingdom.

order.why: Consider the comparison between perception and avoidable danger.
Explains the reinforcing relationship between lust, selfishness, ignorance and harmful action.
Read the reported effect of self-interest on speech.
shortened: The words of many speakers are mixed with the lusts of their souls and their worldly appetites; therefore they will have neither authority nor success.

order.why: Distinguish a religious claim from the conduct that supports it.
shortened: My sorrows are for those who have involved themselves in their corrupt passions, and claim to be associated with the Faith of God, the Gracious, the All-Praised.

order.why: Keep the sharp statement about conduct and belonging attributed.
Read the reported danger of spoiling one’s work.
Turn the examination inward through confession.
shortened: I testify, O my God, that I have put away Thy commandments, and clung to  the dictates of my passions, and have cast away the statutes of Thy Book, and seized the book of mine own desire.

order.why: Join guiding others with restraining oneself.
Read the direction toward revealed guidance.
shortened: The All-Glorious forbiddeth vain desire and commandeth you to observe that which the Lord of all beings hath revealed in His perspicuous Book.

order.why: Connect that direction with recognition and response.
Consider the influence of other people’s motives.
shortened: Beware lest the intimations of such as have been heedless of God through following the promptings of self and desire debar you.

order.why: Read the warning concerning desire as an obstacle.
shortened: And woe unto him whom vain desires have kept back from God, the Lord of the first and the last.

order.why: Turn toward companionship awakened by mercy.
Keep the mystical description beside the compilation’s ethical commands.
shortened: Were I to explain in detail, a book would not suffice and I would not be able to fulfill it, just as that divine mystic and knower of divine mysteries, the lordly Imam, mentioned a drop from these stations in defining the world of the heart, which has surely come to your noble attention - that the final rank of these three stations is the journey from God unto God. In this station and rank, existence is effaced from self and subsists through the Truth. All are from God and unto God shall they return, and "Say: All things are from God" is sufficient witness and adequate proof of this point, as the mystic of Rum has said:

His attributes are annihilated in the attributes of Him
While His essence remains through the survival of His essence

This station certainly has no rules and seeks no customs, meaning all His deeds are pure justice even if outwardly they appear as injustice, and pure knowledge even if in form they appear as ignorance.

order.why: Read knowledge, love, and virtues as means of resistance.
Hear the prayer for protection and steadfastness.
shortened: We beseech God to protect His loved ones from the hosts of self and passion, draw them nigh unto the Most Exalted Horizon, and inspire them with that which will make them daysprings of steadfastness amidst all created things.

order.why: Consider the reported hope for emancipation.
shortened: Our hope is that they be delivered from the clutches of their carnal desires and emancipated from the bondage of self and passion.

order.why: Connect the restraint of passion with benefit in both worlds.
shortened: We have forbidden all from the promptings of self and passion, and have enjoined upon them that which shall profit them in the world to come and in this world.

order.why: Read the call to honorable and enduring activity.
shortened: Man must not follow the dictate of his passion and lust but always be engaged in that which is honorable and enduring.

order.why: Discover the precious capacities beneath the clay.
End the linked readings with joy that attracts others.
shortened: Remember Him with joy and radiance that the people of the contingent world may be attracted thereby - they who have been seized by the intoxication of their desires in such wise as to be shut out from the straight path of God.

order.why: Read the supplied image of education revealing hidden steel.
Close with the supplied invitation to relinquish obstructing attachments.

questions: How does the image of the conquered ruler challenge familiar ideas of freedom and success?
In what ways can desire shape what a person is willing or able to recognize?
How do knowledge, love, education, and prayer contribute differently to the cultivation of restraint?
What does Epictetus’s pause before pleasure illuminate, and how does it compare with the passages’ reliance on divine assistance?
How might we examine our own motives without turning the texts into a means of judging other people’s worth?

references.label: 1 · Epictetus, Enchiridion 34 · Pause before consenting to pleasure
references.note: In Elizabeth Carter’s translation, section 34 recommends a delay before yielding to an anticipated pleasure and reflection on its aftermath. Compare this exercise of attention with the passages on discernment and self-command. The Baha’i texts also emphasize divine guidance, love, and education, giving the comparison further dimensions to examine.

subjects.displayTitle: Praying for unity: learning to become companions
subjects.introduction: Make these separate letters into perfect words, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays, and the request contains a whole theology of unity: letters mean nothing alone, and people are made to be read together. Prayers for unity in the Bahá’í writings ask for scattered sheep to find their shepherd, dispersed birds their gatherer, torn things their mending; for a gathering’s tangled affairs to be set in order, for hatred to go out like a fire, for Turk and Tajik, East and West, to become intimate companions and strangers to cease being called strangers. The petitions move from a single marriage or meeting outward to the whole human family, and they bind inward freedom from self and passion to outward kindness and sweet speech. An ancient Vedic hymn joins common speech, common purpose and common worship in a kindred way [1], from within its own devotional world. To pray these words is to be asked what one must heal, relinquish or learn before companionship can grow. The path continues into unity itself, into the oneness of humanity, and into the wider life of prayer.
subjects.arc: Begin with separate letters finding meaning together, move through healing and reconciliation, then widen from particular bonds toward the fellowship of humanity.

order.why: Read the work of gathering and mending.
shortened: O Lord! Unite all that is scattered and unify all that is divided and mend all that is torn, and gather Thy loved ones in assemblies of remembrance and praise, and admit Thy servants into gatherings of light and glory, and make them a single tongue speaking Thy praise and attributes among the concourse of creation, steadfast in Thy covenants among the people, humble, submissive, proclaiming, devoted, and supplicating to Thy Most Glorious Kingdom, beseeching Thy most exalted horizon.

order.why: Open with separate letters becoming meaningful words.
shortened: O Lord! Make these separate letters into perfect words, and these brief utterances into manifest verses, that they may become conclusive proofs and precedent mercy and transcendent truth and abundant blessing. Make them exalted lamps and keys to the gates of righteousness, stars of guidance and shooting stars against self and passion, outpouring truth and pulsing veins and arteries, trees in Thy garden and flowers in Thy rose-garden.

order.why: Connect unity with healing distressed hearts.
Consider companionship expressed through sweet speech.
Attend to the practical scattering of a gathering’s affairs.
shortened: O Lord! These are a gathering whom Thou hast united through Thy grace; gather their scattered affairs through Thy bounty; strengthen their loins through Thy beneficence; fortify their backs through Thy favors.

order.why: Ask how distance may become nearness.
Keep oppression and forced dispersion visible.
Read reunion through the power of the Covenant.
shortened: Bring them together again, O Lord, by the Power of Thy Covenant, and gather their dispersion by the Might of Thy Promise, and unite their hearts by the dominion of Thy Love!

order.why: Hear the desire to extinguish hatred.
Connect the removal of discord with conduct that guides.
Read the image of becoming one soul.
Consider unity’s relationship to fitting conduct.
shortened: I beseech Thee, moreover, O my God, to unite the hearts of Thy loved ones and to join them together in harmony and fellowship in Thy Cause, that naught may appear from them that would ill beseem them in Thy days.

order.why: Examine freedom from self and passion.
Ask for purification, knowledge, and attentive hearing.
Read reunion as the removal of a veil.
Gather beneath the tree and attend to its life.
shortened: I beseech Thee, by Thine own Self and by Him Whom Thou has appointed as the Manifestation of Thine own Being and Thy discriminating Word unto all that are in heaven and on earth, to gather together Thy servants beneath the shade of the Tree of Thy gracious providence. Help them, then, to partake of its fruits, to incline their ears to the rustling of its leaves, and to the sweetness of the voice of the Bird that chanteth upon its branches.

order.why: Return to the tree’s shade and renewing rain.
shortened: O my God, my God! I beseech Thee to gather Thy loved ones beneath the shade of the Tree of Thy providence, then rain down upon them from the heaven of Thy mercy the showers of Thy glory and bounty.

order.why: Connect gathering with hearing the divine call.
Read the quickening of hearts under grace.
Hear the petition for nearness in every condition.
Imagine meeting face to face.
Consider the blessing of a particular union.
Read marriage as a sign of harmony.
shortened: Suffer them to become the signs of Thy Name in Thy world and protect them through Thy bestowals which are inexhaustible in this world and the world to come. O Lord! They are supplicating the kingdom of Thy mercifulness and invoking the realm of Thy singleness. Verily, they are married in obedience to Thy command. Cause them to become the signs of harmony and unity until the end of time.

order.why: Widen agreement toward human unity.
shortened: "O my God! Unite the hearts of Thy loved ones, make Thy friends' souls one, cause them to be united and in agreement in all matters. Gather them at the fountain of Thy mercy among Thy creatures and beneath the banner of Thy oneness among Thy creation. Assemble them under the standard of human unity and protect them in the shelter of Thy protection from every affliction.

order.why: Connect the community’s concord with its common purpose.
Hear the inclusive enumeration of those to be united.
Join unity of hearts with understanding purpose.
Ask what becomes possible through unity.
A prayer asking divine assistance for loved ones to achieve unity and harmony.
Consider many waves sharing one sea.
shortened: O Lord! Make Thy loved ones waves of the sea of Thy oneness, and breezes from the gardens of Thy singleness, and stars of the heaven of fellowship and love, and pearls of the oceans of love and guidance, that they may drink from a single spring and inhale a single air and be illumined by a single ray and turn with their whole being toward the world of detachment and the center of unity.

order.why: Bring justice into the illumination of hearts.
Read the struggle against discord through spiritual imagery.
Connect unity with faithful observance.
Read the desire for guidance and readiness to act.
Move from remembrance toward service.
Include the support needed for shared endeavors.
shortened: O Lord! These are distinguished servants who have arisen to spread the lights of guidance in those vast regions. O Lord! Fulfill their hopes, assist their supporters, refine their meanings and reward their endeavors.

order.why: Make the one praying a participant in the desired unity.
Extend love and loyalty to all peoples.
Consider the promotion of concord among diverse kindreds.
Join human oneness with universal peace.
Hear the reported invitation to sustained supplication.
shortened: Likewise, we must ever supplicate that God may create love in hearts. Let us implore and beseech that the Sun of Truth may shine upon all, that we may all be immersed in the ocean of the Lord's mercy. Let us implore and beseech that all who are imperfect may become perfect. Let us implore and beseech that all children may reach maturity. May the sun of love shine upon East and West, and may all hearts be illumined by the light of the love of God, and may all souls be quickened by the spirit of divine bestowals.

order.why: Close the linked prayers with estrangement becoming companionship.
shortened: May the East embrace the West, may Europe hasten without delay along the path of love, may the Turk consider the Tajik an intimate companion and count him as dear and kind. May all associate and consort with one another in the utmost fellowship and unity. May estrangement vanish, may mention of others as strangers cease, and may all become familiar friends and compassionate companions to each other. O Lord! Transform this dark night into radiant day, and change this hatred and enmity between nations into fellowship and love, so that the world of creation may find rest and this proud world may seek abundant portion from the divine realm.

order.why: Return to the striking image of opposites brought together.
End with the supplied prayer for protected and harmonized hearts.

questions: What different aspects of unity emerge through letters, waves, birds, trees, and light?
How do prayers for particular people and gatherings open toward the whole human family?
What connections do these prayers make between freedom from self-interest, justice, and fellowship?
How does the Rig Vedic hymn’s common purpose compare with the forms of unity sought here?
What changes in speech, listening, or shared action might give practical expression to these petitions?

neighbors.invitation: Explore how prayers for concord relate to the oneness of humanity.

references.label: 1 · Rig Veda 10.191.2–4 · Assembly and common purpose
references.note: In Ralph T. H. Griffith’s translation, the hymn calls for shared speech, purpose, and resolve within an assembly and its worship. Compare its devotional language of concord with the images in these prayers. Ask how shared purpose relates to the wider Baha’i horizon of fellowship among peoples, while preserving each text’s own setting.

subjects.displayTitle: Reward and punishment: justice, conscience, and love
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh describes the tent of world order as resting on two pillars, reward and punishment, and few images are at once so plain and so searching. Justice, He teaches, means giving each soul its due, and its force restrains the wicked and shelters the weak. Yet ‘Abdu’l-Bahá draws a clear line: society may punish in order to deter, but no individual has the right to revenge, and the one who has been wronged is praised for forgiving. Confucius, too, observed that people driven only by penalties learn to evade them, while those led by virtue come to feel shame and grow good [1]. Beneath public order lies a quieter question about motive. The Báb asks for worship so pure that it would not change whether it led to the fire or to paradise, love offered for God’s sake alone. From here the path opens toward the balance of justice and mercy, the bond between government and the governed, and the place of faith in forming conscience, where fear and hope give way to a devotion that seeks no payment.
subjects.arc: Begin with a deed as its own reward, examine public accountability and its limits, then distinguish revenge, justice, conscience, and disinterested devotion.

order.why: Read worship freed from bargaining over paradise and fire.
shortened: Worship thou God in such wise that if thy worship lead thee to the fire, no alteration in thine adoration would be produced, and so likewise if thy recompense should be paradise. Thus and thus alone should be the worship which befitteth the one True God.
Fire and paradise both bow down and prostrate themselves before God. That which is worthy of His Essence is to worship Him for His sake, without fear of fire, or hope of paradise.

order.why: Open with the relation between recompense and a deed’s intrinsic worth.
shortened: Likewise apprehend thou the nature of hell-fire and be of them that truly believe. For every act performed there shall be a recompense according to the estimate of God, and unto this the very ordinances and prohibitions prescribed by the Almighty amply bear witness. For surely if deeds were not rewarded and yielded no fruit, then the Cause of God - exalted is He - would prove futile. Immeasurably high is He exalted above such blasphemies! However, unto them that are rid of all attachments a deed is, verily, its own reward.

order.why: Define justice through each person’s due.
Explains recompense through the preservation and embodiment of deeds and acquired attributes in each world.
Place reward and punishment within justice and wisdom.
shortened: The Great Being saith:  The structure of world stability and order hath been reared upon, and will continue to be sustained by, the twin pillars of reward and punishment.  And in another connection He hath uttered the following in the eloquent tongue: Justice hath a mighty force at its command.  It is none other than reward and punishment for the deeds of men. By the power of this force the tabernacle of order is established throughout the world, causing the wicked to restrain their natures for fear of punishment.

order.why: Read the pillars beside consultation and compassion.
Consider the origins of hope and fear in moral life.
Retain the concise statement of the twin pillars.
Connect those pillars with public virtues and security.
shortened: Man has been and continues to be among the greatest signs of God, and has come from the realm of non-existence into the court of existence for the knowledge and betterment of the world. Should the leaders of government and nation manifest spiritual virtues, goodly deeds, and kindly words, the lights of justice will encompass all the earth, and all will dwell in perfect tranquility within the pavilion of security and peace. The foundation of the security and welfare of nations rests upon two pillars: reward and punishment. Every sovereign must implement these two principles; indeed it is essential.

order.why: Read the promise addressed to a just ruler.
shortened: Shouldst thou cause rivers of justice to spread their waters amongst thy subjects, God would surely aid thee with the hosts of the unseen and of the seen, and would strengthen thee in thine affairs.

order.why: Keep the particular responsibility of rulers visible.
Recognize the incompleteness of a world without justice.
shortened: And among the teachings of Baha'u'llah are justice and right. Until these are realized on the plane of existence, all things shall be in disorder and remain imperfect. The world of mankind is a world of oppression and cruelty, and a realm of aggression and error.

order.why: Read the reported argument about an official’s motives critically.
shortened: Should an official, on the contrary, think that all responsibility for his actions must end with his earthly life, knowing and believing nothing of Divine favors and a spiritual kingdom of joy, he will lack the incentive to just dealing, and the inspiration to destroy oppression and unrighteousness.

When a ruler knows that his judgments will be weighed in a balance by the Divine Judge, and that if he be not found wanting he will come into the Celestial Kingdom and that the light of the Heavenly Bounty will shine upon him, then will he surely act with justice and equity. Behold how important it is that Ministers of State should be enlightened by religion!

order.why: Distinguish outward deterrence from inward restraint.
Examine the link between wisdom and moral accountability.
shortened: Glory be to Him Who spoke this supreme word: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of God," for the fear and awe of God restraineth man from whatsoever causeth abasement and degradation of the human station, and aideth him in that which leadeth to elevation and glory. The wise man avoideth shameful deeds, for he beholdeth punishment in their wake. The pavilion of world order is upheld upon two pillars: Reward and Punishment.

order.why: Face the criticism of punishment that worsens character.
shortened: Consider how many prisons and dungeons and places of punishment and chastisement are prepared for mankind, that through these coercive means souls may be prevented from committing grievous crimes. Yet this coercion and punishment leads to the increase of evil character, and the desired result is not achieved as it should be.

order.why: Distinguish public protection from personal revenge.
shortened: Question: Should a criminal be punished, or should he be forgiven and his crime overlooked?

Answer: There are two kinds of retributive actions: one is revenge and retaliation and the other, punishment and requital. An individual has no right to seek revenge, but the body politic has the right to punish the criminal. Such punishment is intended to dissuade and deter others from committing similar crimes. It is for the protection of the rights of man and does not constitute revenge, for revenge is that inner gratification that results from returning like for like.

order.why: Consider reason, accountability, and the victim’s freedom to forgive.
shortened: Thus, the prohibitions on murder, theft, treachery, falsehood, hypocrisy, and iniquity are based on reason: Every rational mind can grasp that these are all vile and reprehensible.

As for the body politic, it punishes the aggressor but not to exact revenge. The purpose of this punishment, rather, is to deter and dissuade, and to oppose iniquity and aggression, so as to prevent others from extending their hand likewise in oppression. But if the victim chooses to forgive and to show instead the greatest mercy, this is most approved in the sight of God.

order.why: Read the distinction between vengeance and just chastisement.
shortened: One is vengeance and the other is chastisement. Vengeance is reprehensible and takes place according to one's self and desire. This is a penalty that the selfish ones inflict for the love or purpose of retaliation. Chastisement however, if happens according to divine law in absolute fairness and justice will be rewarding and the cause of good. Because in doing such, that person has executed the divine ordinances and not one's selfish desires.

order.why: Keep the reported reiteration of that distinction.
Retain the reported treatment of intent and severe punishment as reported.
shortened: But the willful murderer, one who looks for his victim with the intent to kill, shall be punished. For instance, he may climb on a wall and watch for his victim, then jump down and kill him; this is murder with intent to kill. In the book (Kitubal-Akdas) it is specified that such a one shall be killed.
It is impossible to protect society unless he is punished. It is not for revenge. God alone has the right to revenge. This punishment is for an example, so that others may not do likewise.

order.why: Distinguish the further recollection and its account of penitence.
Read the reported connection with education and care for the poor.
Balance fear of wrongdoing with hope of pardon.
Consider consequences as mirrors of deeds.
shortened: Had all the peoples of the world hearkened to the Word of Unity as it deserveth to be hearkened to, all would have turned unto God, detached from all else. The deceptive conditions and allusions of the world have debarred the nations from the most great bounty. Reward and punishment are two mirrors reflecting good and evil deeds which are manifested therein.

order.why: Read the return of an action’s consequence to its agent.
Consider the passage’s appeal to volition.
Keep the contrast concerning the direction of one’s actions.
shortened: In this state it is ascribed unto truth and returneth unto Him; otherwise it is reckoned among the followers of self and passion and returneth unto them.

order.why: Read the particular account of self-inflicted chastisement.
shortened: Had the world been of any worth in His sight, He surely would never have allowed His enemies to possess it, even to the extent of a grain of mustard seed. He hath, however, caused you to be entangled with its affairs, in return for what your hands have wrought in His Cause. This, indeed, is a chastisement which ye, of your own will, have inflicted upon yourselves, could ye but perceive it.

order.why: Return to the spiritual horizon of accountability.
Read the supplied attribution to Rabi‘a as a distinct testimony.
Close with the supplied version joining responsibility and hope.

questions: How can a deed be its own reward while reward and punishment also sustain social order?
What differences between justice and revenge do the passages ask us to recognize?
How might consequences protect people yet fail to cultivate character, as one selection warns?
How does the Analects’ distinction between avoiding penalties and becoming good compare with inward and outward restraint here?
What different foundations for moral responsibility appear in the discussions of reason, religion, conscience, and love?
How can a community maintain accountability while leaving room for repentance, mercy, and forgiveness?

neighbors.invitation: Continue examining the relationship between accountability and mercy.

references.label: 1 · Analects 2.3 · Avoiding punishment and becoming good
references.note: James Legge’s translation contrasts governing through penalties with leading through virtue and propriety. Compare the difference between outward compliance and the formation of character with the passages on deterrence and inward restraint. This comparison raises questions about education and example without settling the distinct issue of public protection.

subjects.introduction: The rich should spend their substance for the poor, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá teaches, but of their own free will, for a good deed done under compulsion perfects no one. This voluntary sharing He ranks above equality itself: not preferring oneself to others, even to the point of sacrificing life and property, as the believers in Persia were already doing. Yet He refuses to leave the matter to private generosity. Without just legislation the welfare of the commonwealth cannot be secured, so he pictures laws under which no one is afflicted with poverty and no one holds extreme wealth, a tax proportioned to what a person produces beyond his needs, a village storehouse, and salaries paid in full on the first of the month. Between the forced equality of the socialists and the absolute freedom of laissez-faire, Shoghi Effendi writes, the Cause keeps a balance, and it offers principles to be studied rather than a finished system. The believers in Acts, of one heart and one soul, distributing to each according to need, show what fellowship can make possible and what it requires of trust [1]. From here the inquiry moves toward the moderation of wealth inequality, the nature of justice, the practice of generosity, and a frank look at capitalism, communism and socialism alike.
subjects.arc: Begin with freely chosen sharing, join transformed motives with just institutions, examine livelihoods and practical arrangements, then close with cautions about applying principles.

order.why: Read the account of voluntary sharing beyond formal equality.
shortened: And among the teachings of Baha'u'llah is voluntary sharing of one's property with others among mankind. This voluntary sharing is greater than equality, and consists in this, that man should not prefer himself to others, but rather should sacrifice his life and property for others. But this should not be introduced by coercion so that it becomes a law and man is compelled to follow it. Nay, rather, man should voluntarily and of his own choice sacrifice his property and life for others, and spend willingly for the poor, just as is done in Persia among the Baha'is.

order.why: Open with sharing as a freely chosen moral act.
Explains why economic arrangements should begin with the farmer before extending to other classes.
Consider giving as thanksgiving.
shortened: The patient poor are better than the thankful rich. But the thankful poor are better than the patient poor. And the best of all is the rich-giver who is free from temptations or tests, who becomes the cause of the happiness of mankind. Though through thankgiving blessings are increased, yet the most perfect thanksgiving is through giving, and the station of giving is the highest of all stations. Just as it is said in the Qur'an, 'Ye shall never receive blessings until ye give of that which ye love.'

order.why: Bring the question to an encounter with someone in need.
shortened: Abdul-Baha: "The Friends must strive and show efforts and assist. Whosoever is a believer and assured, firm in the Cause, there is no doubt that he will contribute towards the assistance of the poor. This is an evidence of the faith. But if a person comes in contact with another who is in the utmost need, and he sees that he can help, and if he fails, this is an evidence of the weakness of his faith.

order.why: Join changed hearts with legislative administration.
shortened: The governments will enact these laws, establishing just legislation and economics in order that all humanity may enjoy a full measure of welfare and privilege; but this will always be according to legal protection and procedure. Without legislative administration, rights and demands fail, and the welfare of the commonwealth cannot be realized.

Hearts must be so cemented together, love must become so dominant that the rich shall most willingly extend assistance to the poor and take steps to establish these economic adjustments permanently. If it is accomplished in this way, it will be most praiseworthy because then it will be for the sake of God and in the pathway of His service. For example, it will be as if the rich inhabitants of a city should say, "It is neither just nor lawful that we should possess great wealth while there is abject poverty in this community," and then willingly give their wealth to the poor, retaining only as much as will enable them to live comfortably.

order.why: Read the reported twofold approach of hearts and laws.
shortened: Tell Mrs. D. there are only two ways of correcting the social conditions: it cannot be force. One is changing the hearts of the people, so that those who have great wealth will give freely and gladly. The other is by executing new and just laws which will regulate all the economic conditions, so that there will not be the extremes, the very rich nor the very poor.

order.why: Consider legal measures against extreme inequality.
shortened: Nevertheless, it is not right that some should be extremely wealthy while others extremely poor. It must be improved and such laws established that all have comfort and wellbeing - neither should one be afflicted with poverty nor another have extreme wealth. For example, a wealthy person who has utmost wealth should not let another person have utmost poverty, but should take care of them so they too can be comfortable. This must be implemented through laws. The wealthy must themselves give their excess wealth to the poor, and likewise the country's laws must be such that by God's law everyone has comfort.

order.why: Keep the reported insistence on justice without violence.
shortened: But it must be solved with justice and not with force. If this problem is not solved lovingly it will result in war. Perfect communism and equality are an impossibility because they would upset the affairs and the order of the world. But there is a fair method which will not leave the poor in such need, nor the rich in such wealth.

The rich should be merciful to the poor, but with their free-will, not with force. Should it be with force it would be useless. It should be according to law and not by violence, so that through a general law everyone might know his duty.

order.why: Address the relation of labor and capital through mutual sacrifice.
Read religious obligation together with inward willingness.
Distinguish differences of function from deprivation.
Consider the reported aim of shared welfare.
Examine the illustrative relation between capacity, need, and taxation.
shortened: Each person in the community whose need is equal to his individual producing capacity shall be exempt from taxation. But if his income is greater than his needs, he must pay a tax until an adjustment is effected. That is to say, a man's capacity for production and his needs will be equalized and reconciled through taxation. If his production exceeds, he will pay a tax; if his necessities exceed his production, he shall receive an amount sufficient to equalize or adjust. Therefore, taxation will be proportionate to capacity and production, and there will be no poor in the community.

order.why: Read the proposed village storehouse.
Consider the reported arrangements for productive assistance.
Notice the concrete importance of reliable payment.
Read the reported administration of contributions.
shortened: To record contributions from those who are real Bahais - no one else is asked to contribute and no collections are taken at general meetings; and there are certain times appointed for receiving Bahai contributions and giving of receipts. To determine how such funds shall be spent; how much for teaching, how much for relief of the poor and so forth. Especially in the case of anonymous gifts, which are frequently received.

order.why: Keep the demanding reported language about independence in its setting.
shortened: The work must attain such a pitch that should a wealthy person offer a gift to a poor man, the poor man should feel himself independent and not accept it. The time must come and the work get so high that every community will have a box for charity which may be full to the brim of gold and yet a poor man will refuse to take any so long as he is able to work for himself. The work must reach such a pitch.
But the world will reach a state wherein neither absolute poverty nor great wealth will exist. Giving should be a joy to the giver, however poor he maybe, or however small his gift.

order.why: Hear the reported challenge to industrial servitude.
Read the historical criticism of labor and military expenditure as attributed.
Consider financiers’ responsibility concerning aggressive war.
Keep the reported profit-sharing forecast distinct from an enacted rule.
shortened: It will not be possible in the future for men to amass great fortunes by the labor of others. The rich will willingly divide. They will come to this gradually, naturally, by their own volition. It will never be accomplished by war and bloodshed. The ruling power or government cannot treat the rich unjustly. To force them to divide their wealth would be unjust. In the future, proportionately about three-quarters of the profits will go to the workmen and one-quarter to the owner. This condition will prevail in about one century. It will certainly come to pass.

order.why: Read the reported expectation of leisure from machinery.
shortened: The labor saving machines were given to create leisure for all mankind... The first decided shortening of the hours will appear when a legal working day of eight hours is established... But this working day of eight hours is only the beginning. Soon there will be a six hour day, a five hour, a three hour day, even less than that, and the worker must be paid more for this management of machines, than he ever received for the exercise of his two hands alone.

order.why: Retain the reported forecast of conflict with its historical limitations.
shortened: Where there is an agitation of the masses, it will not be quieted, until it reaches its climax. At last, things will come to such a state that they will say: 'The factories belong to us and the capitalists will get their share from us.' It will come to that. 'We will apportion the share they ought to receive, for instance, one-tenth.' They will take nine-tenths. Everything will become chaotic. At last it will reach such a state that the world of humanity will come to an absolute stand-still. Even the labourer will go hungry. Then absolutism will return, so that the Government may remedy it.
Nothing save the Religion of God will solve it. Nothing save the Religion of God. This will include both; the capitalists and labourers will be freed.

order.why: Consider the letter’s concern with a unifying moral power.
Read the reported connection with heart and spirit.
Retain the further claim concerning faith and contentment.
Examine the reported comparison with compulsory equality.
shortened: The principles of socialism are outstripped in the religions of God. For instance, God commands, 'But [they] prefer them [the poor] before themselves, although there be indigence among them' [Q59:9]. That is, the believers spend of their substance and share their possessions and prefer others to themselves willingly and with utmost spirituality. Socialists, however, desire to enforce equality and association by compulsion.

order.why: Return to the transformation of hearts amid claims of right.
Read cooperation as the basis of enduring change.
Keep the supplied comparison of willing and enforced sharing.
Read the supplied warning against both economic extremes.
Distinguish the supplied pilgrim notes from authoritative legislation.
Consider the later letter’s distinction between principles and a technical system.
End with the responsibility to study application rather than conjecture.

questions: How do voluntary sharing and just legislation support or challenge one another in these selections?
What would it mean to preserve dignity while ensuring that everyone’s basic needs are met?
How do the practical examples of taxation, credit, wages, and contributions help us think beyond general goodwill?
What similarities and differences emerge when the distribution according to need in Acts is read beside these passages?
How should the reported proposals, forecasts, pilgrim notes, and later letters be weighed when developing an application?
What kinds of study, consultation, and experience would help translate a spiritual principle into a workable economic arrangement?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the institutions and relationships that moderate economic extremes.

references.label: 1 · Acts 4:32–35 · Fellowship and distribution according to need
references.note: The community’s unity of heart is expressed through shared possessions and distribution to meet need. Compare the relation between fellowship and material provision with the passages on giving and economic adjustment. Acts describes a particular community; it does not supply a ready-made blueprint for the laws and institutions discussed here.

subjects.displayTitle: The mystery of suffering: compassion and the limits of explanation
subjects.introduction: Some lives are cut short or hemmed in by handicap and trial before they have been lived to the full, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says plainly that this is a cause for grieving. Infants are innocent and rest under the shadow of divine favour; the lament of Bahá’u’lláh over calamity falling like thunderbolts is allowed its full cry. Only then do distinctions appear. Some suffering is the harvest of our own conduct; some belongs to the exigencies of a changing world; some is a trial through which the faithful, like Christ and the apostles, attain their greatest perfection. Over it all stands an admission that human minds cannot encompass every divine purpose, and the image of a gardener moving a tender shrub to wider ground while onlookers think he has torn it up in anger. Job’s friends, rebuked for not speaking rightly of God, warn against confident explanations delivered to a person in pain [1]. The question opens outward into tests and trials, the mystery of sacrifice, and the claim that evil has no existence of its own.
subjects.arc: Begin with acknowledged grief and innocence, distinguish sources of suffering, then explore wisdom and hope while preserving the limits of explanation and the voice of lament.

order.why: Read the response to a particular disaster as situated exhortation.
shortened: Those were indeed dire events in San Francisco. Disasters of this kind should serve to awaken the people, and diminish the love of their hearts for this inconstant world. It is in this nether world that such tragic things take place: this is the cup that yieldeth bitter wine.

order.why: Open with acknowledgment that diminished lives are a cause for grief.
shortened: As to those souls who are born into this life as ethereal and radiant entities and yet, on account of their handicaps and trials, are deprived of great and real advantages, and leave the world without having lived to the full -- certainly this is a cause for grieving. This is the reason why the universal Manifestations of God unveil Their countenances to man, and endure every calamity and sore affliction, and lay down Their lives as a ransom; it is to make these very people, the ready ones, the ones who have capacity, to become dawning points of light, and to bestow upon them the life that fadeth never.

order.why: Affirm infants’ innocence before discussing explanations.
shortened: Infants are under the shadow of the favor of God, and as they have not committed any sin and are not soiled with the impurities of the world of nature, they are centers of the manifestation of bounty, and the Eye of Compassion will be turned upon them.

order.why: Consider the many forms of human sorrow.
Give full space to the language of lament.
Read creation’s sympathy with the afflicted.
shortened: Thou hearest the sighing of atoms and the groaning of all created things by reason of what hath befallen Thy chosen ones and trusted ones, who cast the world behind their backs in Thy days and were so transported by the sweet stream of divine knowledge that they offered up their very souls in Thy path.

order.why: Distinguish misconduct from the conditions of contingent existence.
Read the reported distinction beside the suffering of Christ and the apostles.
shortened: The trials of man are of two kinds. (a) The consequences of his own actions. If a man eats too much, he ruins his digestion; if he takes poison he becomes ill or dies. If a person gambles he will lose his money; if he drinks too much he will lose his equilibrium. All these sufferings are caused by the man himself, it is quite clear therefore that certain sorrows are the result of our own deeds. (b) Other sufferings there are, which come upon the Faithful of God. Consider the great sorrows endured by Christ and by His apostles!
Those who suffer most, attain to the greatest perfection.

order.why: Consider the difference between trial and retribution.
shortened: Know thou that ordeals are of two kinds: One kind is for trial (to test the soul), and the other is punishment for actions. ("As a man soweth so shall he reap.") That which is for testing is educational and developmental and that which is the punishment of deeds is severe retribution.

order.why: Keep the reported account of moral evil distinct from all suffering.
Read the reported account of imperfection and the lower nature.
shortened: Abdu'l-Baha. -- 'Evil is imperfection. Sin is the state of man in the world of the baser nature, for in nature exist defects such as injustice, tyranny, hatred, hostility, strife: these are characteristics of the lower plane of nature. These are the sins of the world, the fruits of the tree from which Adam did eat.

order.why: Consider the reported goodness of things in their proper setting.
Retain the reported distinction concerning human responses and divine affliction.
shortened: There are two kinds of afflictions, the first is human, the second is divine. Human affliction can be coped with and eradicated by human agencies and methods but when an affliction is brought down upon mankind, occasioned by their utter heedlessness and negligence the displaying of all their available forces will not be crowned with the least success.

order.why: Name the three reported mysteries without claiming to solve them.
shortened: The Lord God pleased to give the human being three great mysteries (secrets, riddles) on his journey through life. The final unveiling of them will only occur when our soul has shed its earthly body. The three mysteries are:
1. The great mystery of good and evil.
2. The mystery of the suffering of infants and of the animal (i.e. of the innocent creature).
3. The mystery of the human right to self-determination - of free will.
All great Revealers (Manifestations of God), be it Moses, Christ, Muhammad, Baha'u'llah etc show that these three difficult questions are related to each other.

order.why: Keep the reported acknowledgment of theological obscurity.
Read the deliberate limitation to one kind of suffering.
shortened: The purpose and goal of human suffering is manifold, and if we were to discuss the mysteries of the almighty and all-wise Creator until nightfall, we would hardly get beyond the beginning! So let us this once limit ourselves and consider only one kind of suffering, the suffering which is meant as purification.

order.why: Attend to the limits of the human mind.
shortened: The consummate wisdom of God, however, is manifold and not every soul is apprised of its mysteries. Indeed, His all-encompassing mercy and His all-embracing wisdom entail certain exigencies that transcend the ken of human mind. Sorrow not, then, if trials, tribulations and adversities wax ever more severe, for the grace and bestowals of God are likewise unceasing.

order.why: Preserve the brief statement of hidden wisdom.
shortened: In truth, what has occurred is among the hidden mysteries and consummate wisdom. Verily thy Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

order.why: Keep the fragmentary source’s language and omissions visible.
Read confidence alongside the acknowledgment of mystery.
Consider the expectation of reasons not yet understood.
shortened: Verily, the will of God engages occasionally in some matter for which mankind is unable to find out the reason. The causes and reasons shall appear.

order.why: Uses a Quranic account of adversity to explain tribulation as a means of spiritual attainment.
Keep the reported personal testimony distinct from a general rule for illness.
Retain the particular statement about life, children, and sustenance.
Read the claim concerning concealment in its own setting.
Face the difficult statement about innocent suffering and recompense.
shortened: As to the subject of babes and infants and weak ones who art afflicted by the hands of oppressors: This contains great wisdom and this subject is of paramount importance. In brief, for those souls there is a recompense in another world and many details are connected with this matter. For those souls that suffering is the greatest mercy of God. Verily that mercy of the Lord is far better and preferable to all the comfort of this world and the growth and development of this place of mortality.

order.why: Consider the gardener’s image as consolation about a wider life.
shortened: The inscrutable divine wisdom underlieth such heartrending occurrences. It is as if a kind gardener transferreth a fresh and tender shrub from a confined place to a wide open area. This transfer is not the cause of the withering, the lessening or the destruction of that shrub; nay, on the contrary, it maketh it to grow and thrive, acquire freshness and delicacy, become green and bear fruit. This hidden secret is well known to the gardener, but those souls who are unaware of this bounty suppose that the gardener, in his anger and wrath, hath uprooted the shrub.

order.why: Read the argument from this life toward a life beyond it.
shortened: When thou lookest about thee with a perceptive eye, thou wilt note that on this dusty earth all humankind are suffering. Here no man is at rest as a reward for what he hath performed in former lives; nor is there anyone so blissful as seemingly to pluck the fruit of bygone anguish.

And just as, if human life in the womb were limited to that uterine world, existence there would be nonsensical, irrelevant---so too if the life of this world, the deeds here done and their fruitage, did not come forth in the world beyond, the whole process would be irrational and foolish.

order.why: Keep the intense language of return to God within its devotional horizon.
Consider detachment amid universal vulnerability.
shortened: Do not think these afflictions and tribulations are confined to you. In truth, all creation is in torment so that they may not become attached to this world and instead seek comfort and rest in the divine world and pursue heavenly gifts.

order.why: Read the hope placed beyond the transient world.
shortened: The world hath ever been the abode of tribulations and calamities, but since it is transient, sorrow is unwarranted, for everlasting divine blessings and infinite mercies are ordained.

order.why: Hear the counsel concerning matters beyond one’s control.
Hold together confidence in wisdom and acknowledged tears.
shortened: Whatsoever hath come to pass is in conformity with wisdom, and all must needs be content therewith---nay rather, cherish hope in it. Yet in certain matters, when after the sweetness of reunion there cometh the bitterness of separation, and when after nearness and meeting the decree of remoteness is pronounced, it is for this reason that sighs of sorrow and grief are raised and the tears of the eyes are made to flow.

order.why: Consider the reported lamp image and the question of prayer.
Read the relation between error, forgiveness, and mercy.
shortened: O my Lord! O my Lord! Were heedlessness not to exist, how would the standards of Thy mercy be raised and the banners of Thy generosity be unfurled? And were error not to be declared, how would it be known that Thou art the Concealer, the Forgiver, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise?

order.why: Consider the passage concerning negation and affirmation.
shortened: For the letters of negation, no matter how far they may be removed from the holy fragrances of Thy knowledge, and however forgetful they may become of the wondrous splendors of the dawning light of Thy beauty, which are shed from the heaven of Thy majesty, must needs exist in Thy realm, so that the words which affirm Thee may thereby be exalted.

order.why: Hear the Fire Tablet’s relation between calamity and patience.
shortened: Were it not for the cold, how would the heat of Thy words prevail, O Expounder of the worlds?
Were it not for calamity, how would the sun of Thy patience shine, O Light of the worlds?

order.why: Read the reported images of benefits not yet understood.
shortened: Consider how the mother solicitously takes care of the babe, yet because the babe is not aware, it cannot appreciate the tender training showered upon her: instead it whines and cries! Reflect also, what a source of incalculable benefit is the cloud to the earth! It pours down rain and adorns the plains with verdant plants and sweet herbs: yet because the earth is not aware of this paradisical transformation, it cannot appreciate it and thank God for it. This cool breeze that is passing by, gives life to the trees, but they are unconscious of it.

order.why: Allow winter’s transformation into spring to open hope.
Read the claim of spiritual gain under adverse conditions.
shortened: Whatsoever occurreth in the world of being is light for His loved ones and fire for the people of sedition and strife. Even if all the losses of the world were to be sustained by one of the friends of God, he would still profit thereby, whereas true loss would be borne by such as are wayward, ignorant and contemptuous.

The friends of God shall win and profit under all conditions, and shall attain true wealth. In fire they remain cold, and from water they emerge dry. Their affairs are at variance with the affairs of men. Gain is their lot, whatever the deal.

order.why: Close the linked readings with the assurance of divine care.
shortened: Be not dismayed by what hath befallen you through the decree that is established, but rather rejoice in what God hath ordained for you and inscribed as irrevocable in the Mother Book. He ordaineth for His servants only that which is better for them than all the treasures of the heavens and earth, were ye to know it.

order.why: Return to the reported exhortation about purification with its attribution intact.
End with the supplied words from Job and their challenge to knowledge.

questions: How does beginning with grief and innocence affect the way we hear the later explanations?
Why does the distinction between misconduct and the conditions of a changing world matter when considering suffering?
What can the images of the gardener, winter, the womb, and the lamp illuminate, and where might their limits lie?
How do the acknowledgment of mystery and the rebuke of Job’s friends challenge our confidence in explaining another person’s pain?
How might hope beyond this life coexist with compassion and efforts to relieve suffering here?
What differences emerge between finding meaning in one’s own trial and assigning a meaning to someone else’s?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the distinction between voluntary choices and conditions beyond our control.

references.label: 1 · Job 42:7 · The friends’ explanations called into question
references.note: After the divine speeches, God rebukes Eliphaz and his two friends for not speaking rightly about Him as Job has. Read this alongside the supplied excerpt from Job 38 and the compilation’s acknowledgment of hidden wisdom. Consider how the text complicates confident explanations offered to a person in distress.

subjects.displayTitle: Useful work: skill, dignity, and service
subjects.introduction: A craft, a trade, a profession: Bahá’u’lláh raises the daily work of His followers to the rank of worship, and prizes a single coin honestly earned above a treasure amassed by wrong. One of God’s own names, He says, is the Fashioner, and He loves craftsmanship. Dignity, self-assurance and the common good are all at stake, which is why ‘Abdu’l-Bahá insists that every child learn a trade beside book learning, prefers a good carpenter or shoemaker to an idle angel, and takes the trouble to find a printing press job for one man who needs it, making work a shared responsibility rather than a private burden. Detachment, Bahá’u’lláh adds, was never at odds with outward affairs, a claim the Bhagavad Gita’s counsel of action without attachment to its fruits invites us to weigh [1]. What emerges is a picture in which earning, learning, moral growth and contribution feed one another. From here the road leads to work as worship, to the refusal of idleness and mendicancy, and to working for the betterment of the world.
subjects.arc: Begin with work elevated to worship, examine honest means and practical support, then follow training and excellence toward a life of service.

order.why: Open with useful work elevated to worship.
Urges perfection of workmanship and avoidance of waste in both collective and individual crafts.
Read the image of fruitful trees and necessary means.
Consider craftsmanship through the divine name Fashioner.
shortened: One of the names of God is the Fashioner, and He has always loved and continues to love craftsmanship. Therefore, whoever among His servants manifests this name is beloved in the presence of the Wronged One.

order.why: Compare honest earning with wealth acquired wrongly.
Direct abilities toward the general good.
Reject a conflict between detachment and outward affairs.
Connect useful knowledge and useful work.
shortened: It is permissible to study sciences and arts, but such sciences as are useful and would redound to the progress and advancement of the people.

It is enjoined upon every one of you to engage in some form of occupation, such as crafts, trades and the like. We have graciously exalted your engagement in such work to the rank of worship unto God, the True One. Ponder ye in your hearts the grace and the blessings of God and render thanks unto Him at eventide and at dawn. Waste not your time in idleness and sloth. Occupy yourselves with that which profiteth yourselves and others.

order.why: Recognize craftsmen as facilitators of common life.
Read the reported link between vocation and service.
Consider the reported purpose of dignity and self-assurance.
Make access to work a responsibility of assistance.
Read encouragement through kind counsel.
Consider preparation for a useful livelihood.
shortened: He teaches that it is incumbent upon all mankind to become fitted for some useful trade, craft or profession by which subsistence may be assured, and this efficiency is to be considered as an act of worship.

order.why: Hear the hope for acquiring a skill.
Read the reported expectation that every child learn a craft.
shortened: In short, the explicit command of Baha'u'llah is that every child, whether rich or poor, aristocrat or democrat, high or low must learn a trade, an art or a craft. This law must be incorporated in the constitution of every school. Supposing that a person is not in need, that economically speaking he is rich, even he, for the sake of obedience to the blessed command must acquire a profession. A Baha'i must correlate his actions, words and affairs with the basic principles of the Blessed Perfection.

order.why: Examine the reported relation between education and practical ability.
shortened: All the Baha'i children must learn a trade or manual profession. This must be aside from their literary education. The study of foreign languages, such as English, French, German etc must be coupled with the study of an art, craft or profession.

Learn to do something in this world, no matter how small it may be. it is better to be a good carpenter, a fine shoemaker, a skillful physician, an accomplished engineer, an excellent gardener, a brilliant artist, a superior teacher, an inspired writer than to be an angel in heaven with nothing to do but to sing hallelujah and play on golden harp.

order.why: Notice the achievement of children learning a craft amid trials.
Keep the reported counsel for a young person in its particular setting.
shortened: Similarly a young man desiring to lay a good foundation for his later life must devote his first few years to the study of his chosen profession and forget all pleasures and sports which divert him from accomplishing his main purpose. This is success and prosperity.

order.why: Read mat weaving as a concrete example.
Turn from acquisition of skill toward excellence.
Consider devotion to one’s vocation.
Read the encouragement to apply effort.
shortened: Now attend to your craft and apply effort. God willing, work will become organized.

order.why: Keep the practical direction to sustain a shop.
Read the encouragement addressed to a particular recipient.
shortened: All have been commanded to occupy themselves with some affair; therefore that honorable one should engage in some occupation, and blessings shall descend from the heaven of the bounty of thy Lord, the All-Bountiful, the Enriching, the Mighty, the Merciful.

order.why: Retain the brief direction concerning present work.
Read the further encouragement to a named craftsman.
Consider approval of engagement in trade.
Connect livelihood through craft with nearness to God.
Read the relation between work and freedom from expectation.
shortened: Blessed is he who gazeth toward the Most Exalted Horizon and acteth according to the command of the Lord of Names, and blessed is he who in these divine days is engaged in a handicraft. This is a bounty from God, for in this Most Great Revelation engagement in that which preventeth man from expectation is acceptable before God.

order.why: Consider trust alongside the use of means.
Include agriculture within the ordinance.
shortened: Regarding agriculture, He has given a general ruling in these matters, which is that it is obligatory for every soul to engage in a profession, agriculture, or craft, and that very work itself is worship in the sight of God, even if one tarries but a day in any land.

order.why: Retain the concise general direction.
Read its further reiteration.
Keep honest endeavor central.
shortened: As to the affairs of this world: from the heaven of the divine Will the ordinance of gainful occupation and honest endeavor hath been sent down.

order.why: Read the situated advice about company, trade, and prayer.
shortened: Certainly, absolutely be free from such a detestable group and occupy yourself with trade and business, and continually supplicate and implore at the divine threshold, and pray for our good.

order.why: Consider the different pursuits around which lives are organized.
shortened: O ye two who are attracted to the Divine Beauty! Every person in this world is occupied with some pursuit and familiar with some matter. One charges forth in the political arena, another arranges battle formations, another hastens to the field of commerce and industry, and yet another strives mightily to amass worldly ornaments.

order.why: Distinguish moral conduct from merely lacking the power to harm.
Read the reported distinction between uplifting and degrading work.
shortened: You can engage in work of an uplifting kind- the kind that will tend to lift one out of the sense world into the world of morality not the kind that is degrading.

order.why: Consider opportunities for service within outward affairs.
shortened: Today the foundation of all affairs has been and is service to God's Cause, and it is best for His loved ones in every land to engage in outward affairs, for they can thus convey a word of truth to people or render some service to the friends.

order.why: Keep the reported division of time as particular counsel.
Close the linked passages with confidence and joyful engagement.
End with the supplied letter on work and training as means of understanding purpose.

questions: What changes when work is understood through its benefit and honesty rather than its prestige?
How do the passages join individual effort with responsibility to help another person find work?
What relationships emerge among education, practical skill, diligence, and excellence?
How does the Bhagavad Gita’s action without attachment compare with the compatibility of detachment and outward affairs described here?
How might livelihood, service, and the cultivation of virtues strengthen one another in a particular vocation?

neighbors.invitation: Follow useful work into the wider field of service to humanity.
Reflect further on the spiritual meaning of ordinary work.

references.label: 1 · Bhagavad Gita 3.19 · Action without attachment
references.note: In Swami Mukundananda’s translation, the verse commends fulfilling one’s duty without attachment to the fruits of action. Compare this with the passages that unite detachment, practical occupation, and service. Ask what attention to the quality and benefit of work might mean when personal acquisition is no longer its sole measure.
